{{Short description|Mathematical form for PDEs}}
In mathematics, a '''Janet basis''' is a [[canonical form|normal form]] for systems of linear homogeneous [[partial differential equation]]s (PDEs) that removes the inherent arbitrariness of any such system.  It was introduced in 1920 by [[Maurice Janet]].<ref name="Janet">M. Janet, [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101080166299;view=1up;seq=75 Les systèmes d'équations aux dérivées partielles], Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées  '''8 ser., t. 3''' (1920), pages 65–123.</ref>  It was first called the Janet basis by Fritz Schwarz in 1998.<ref name="Schwarz1998">F. Schwarz, [https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=tfa7dpQf1OIC&oi=fnd&pg=PA221 "Janet Bases for Symmetry Groups"], in: ''Gröbner Bases and Applications; Lecture Notes Series'' '''251''', London Mathematical Society, pages 221–234 (1998); B. Buchberger and F. Winkler, Edts.</ref>

The left hand sides of such systems of equations may be considered as differential polynomials of a ring, and Janet's normal form as a special basis of the ideal that they generate. By abuse of language, this terminology will be applied both to the original system and the ideal of differential polynomials generated by the left hand sides. A Janet basis is the predecessor of a [[Gröbner basis]] introduced by [[Bruno Buchberger]]<ref name="Buchberger">B. Buchberger, Ein algorithmisches Kriterium fuer die Loesbarkeit eines algebraischen Gleichungssystems, Aequ. Math. '''4''', 374–383(1970).</ref> for polynomial ideals. In order to generate a Janet basis for any given system of linear PDEs a ranking of its derivatives must be provided; then the corresponding Janet basis is unique. If a system of linear PDEs is given in terms of a Janet basis its differential dimension may easily be determined; it is a measure for the degree of indeterminacy of its general solution. In order to generate a [[Loewy decomposition]] of a system of linear PDEs its Janet basis must be determined first.

== Generating a Janet basis ==

Any system of linear homogeneous PDEs is highly non-unique, e.g. an arbitrary [[linear combination]] of its elements may be added to the system without changing its [[solution set]]. A priori it is not known whether it has any nontrivial solutions. More generally, the degree of arbitrariness of its general solution is not known, i.e. how many undetermined constants or functions it may contain. These questions were the starting point of Janet's work; he considered systems of linear PDEs in any number of dependent and independent variables and generated a normal form for them. Here mainly linear PDEs in the plane with the coordinates <math> x</math> and <math> y</math> will be considered; the number of unknown functions is one or two. Most results described here may be generalized in an obvious way to any number of variables or functions.<ref name="Schwarz2007">F. Schwarz, Algorithmic Lie Theory for Solving Linear Ordinary Differential Equations, Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2007 Chapter 2.</ref><ref name="PleskenRobertz">W. Plesken, D. Robertz, Janet's approach to presentations and resolutions for polynomials and linear pdes, Archiv der Mathematik '''84''', pages 22–37, 2005.</ref><ref name="Oaku">T. Oaku, T. Shimoyama, A Gröbner Basis Method for Modules over Rings of Differential Operators, Journal of Symbolic Computation '''18''', pages 223–248, 1994.</ref>
In order to generate a unique representation for a given system of linear PDEs, at first a ranking of its derivatives must be defined.

'''Definition''':
A ranking of derivatives is a total ordering such that for any two derivatives <math>\delta</math>, <math>\delta_1</math> and
<math>\delta_2</math>, and any derivation operator <math>\theta</math> the relations <math>\delta\leq\theta\delta</math> and
<math>\delta_1\leq\delta_2\rightarrow\delta\delta_1\leq\delta\delta_2</math> are valid.

A derivative <math>\delta_2</math> is called ''higher'' than <math>\delta_1</math> if <math>\delta_2>\delta_1</math>. The highest
derivative in an equation is called its ''leading derivative''. For the derivatives up to order two of a single function <math>z</math> depending on <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> with <math>x>y</math> two possible order are
: the LEX order <math> z_{xx}> z_{xy}> z_x >z_{yy} >z_y >z</math> and the GRLEX order <math>z_{xx} > z_{xy} > z_{yy} > z_x > z_y > z</math>.

Here the usual notation <math>\partial_xz=z_x, \partial_yz=z_y,\ldots </math> is used. If the number of functions is higher than one, these orderings have to be generalized appropriately, e.g. the orderings <math>TOP</math> or <math>POT</math> may be applied.<ref name="Adams">W. Adams, P. Loustaunau, An introduction to Gröbner bases, [[American Mathematical Society]], Providence, 1994.</ref>
The first basic operation to be applied in generating a Janet basis is the ''reduction'' of an equation <math>e_1</math> [[wikt:WRT|w.r.t.]] another one <math>e_2</math>. In colloquial terms this means the following: Whenever a derivative of <math>e_1</math> may be
obtained from the leading derivative of <math>e_2</math> by suitable differentiation, this differentiation is performed and the
result is subtracted from <math>e_1</math>. Reduction w.r.t. a system of PDEs means reduction w.r.t. all elements of the system. A system of linear PDEs is called ''autoreduced'' if all possible reductions have been performed.

The second basic operation for generating a Janet basis is the inclusion  of ''integrability conditions''. They are obtained as follows: If two equations <math>e_1</math> and <math>e_2</math> are such that by suitable differentiations two new equations may be obtained with like leading derivatives, by cross-multiplication with its leading coefficients and subtraction of the resulting equations a new equation is obtained, it is called an integrability condition. If by reduction w.r.t. the remaining equations of the system it does not vanish it is included as a new equation to the system.

It may be shown that repeating these operations always terminates after a finite number of steps with a unique answer which is called the Janet basis for the input system. Janet has organized them in terms of the following algorithm.

'''Janet's algorithm''': Given a system of linear differential polynomials  <math>S\equiv\{e_1,e_2,\ldots \}</math>, the Janet basis corresponding to <math>S</math> is returned.

: S1: (''Autoreduction'') Assign <math>S:=\operatorname{Autoreduce}(S)</math>
: S2: (''Completion'') Assign <math> S:=\operatorname{CompleteSystem}(S)</math>
: S3: (''Integrability conditions'') Find all pairs of leading terms <math>v_i</math> of <math>e_i</math> and <math>v_j</math> of <math>e_j</math> such that differentiation w.r.t. a nonmultiplier <math>x_{i_k}</math> and multipliers  <math>x_{j_1}, \ldots, x_{j_l}</math> leads to <math display="block">\frac{\partial v_i}{\partial x_{i_k}}=\frac{\partial^{p_1+\cdots+p_l}v_j}
 {\partial x_{j_1}^{p_1}\cdots \partial x_{j_l}^{p_l}}</math> and determine the integrability conditions <math display="block">c_{i,j} = \operatorname{Lcoef}(e_j)\cdot
    \frac{\partial e_i}{\partial x_{i_k}} - \operatorname{Lcoef}(e_i)\cdot
   \frac{\partial^{p_1+\cdots+p_l}e_j}
 {\partial x_{j_1}^{p_1}\cdots \partial x_{j_l}^{p_l}}</math>
: S4: (''Reduction of integrability conditions''). For all <math>c_{i,j}</math> assign <math>c_{i,j}:=\operatorname{Reduce}(c_{i,j},S)</math>
: S5: (''Termination?'') If all <math>c_{i,j}</math> are zero return <math>S</math>, otherwise make the assignment <math>S:=S\cup\{c_{i,j}\mid c_{i,j}\neq 0\}</math>, reorder <math>S</math> properly and goto S1

Here <math>Autoreduce</math> is a subalgorithm that returns its argument with all possible reductions performed, <math>Completion</math> adds certain equations to the system in order to facilitate determining the integrability conditions. To this end the variables are divides into ''multipliers'' and ''non-multipliers''; details may be found in the above references. Upon successful termination a Janet basis for the input system will be returned.

'''Example 1''': Let the system <math display="block">\left\{e_1\equiv z_{xy}-\frac{x^2}{y^2}z_x-\frac{x-y}{y^2}z=0, e_2\equiv z_x+\frac{1}{x}z_y+xz=0\right\}</math> be given with ordering GRLEX and <math>x>y</math>.  Step S1 returns the autoreduced system

: <math> \left\{e_3\equiv z_{yy}+\frac 1 {y^2}(xy^3-x^2-y)z_y-\frac 1 y (x^3-x+y)z=0, e_2=z_x+\frac 1 y z_y+xz=0\right\}.</math>

Steps S3 and S4 generate the integrability condition <math>c_{3,2}\equiv\frac{\partial e_3}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial^2e_2}{\partial y^2}</math> and reduces it to <math>z=0</math>, i.e. the Janet basis for the originally given system is <math>\{z=0\}</math> with the trivial solution <math>z=0</math>.

The next example involves two unknown functions <math>w</math> and <math>z</math>, both depending on <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>.

'''Example 2''': Consider the system

:<math>
\begin{align}
\Big\{ & f_1 \equiv w_{xx}-2z_{xy}-\frac{1}{2x}w_x+\frac{1}{2x^2}w=0, f_2\equiv w_{xy}-\frac{1}{2}z_{yy}-\frac{1}{2x}w_y-6x^2z_x, \\[5pt]
& f_3\equiv w_{yy}+4x^2w_x-8x^2z_y-8xw=0, f_4\equiv z_{xx}+\frac{1}{2x}z_x=0\Big\}
\end{align}
</math>

in GRLEX, <math>w>z,x>y</math> ordering. The system is already autoreduced, i.e. step S1 returns it unchanged. Step S3 generates the two integrability conditions

:<math>c_{1,2}\equiv\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}\text{ and }c_{2,3}\equiv\frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x}.</math>

Upon reduction in step S4 they are

:<math>c_{1,2}=z_{xyy}-6xz_x=0, c_{2,3}=z_{yyy}+3x^2z_{xy}-24xz_y-12w=0.</math>

In step S5 they are included into the system and the algorithms starts again with step S1 with the extended system. After a few more iterations finally the Janet basis
<math display="block">\left\{z_y+\frac 1 {2x} w= 0,z_x=0,w_y=0, w_x- \frac 1 x w =0\right\}</math>

is obtained. It yields the general solution <math>z=C_1-C_2 y, w=2C_2 x</math> with two undetermined constants <math>C_1</math> and <math>C_2</math>.

== Application of Janet bases ==

The most important application of a Janet basis is its use for deciding the degree of indeterminacy of a system of linear homogeneous partial differential equations. The answer in the above Example 1 is that the system under consideration allows only the trivial solution. In the second Example 2 a two-dimensional solution space is obtained. In general, the answer may be more involved, there may be infinitely many free constants in the general solution; they may be obtained from the Loewy decomposition of the respective Janet basis.<ref name="Schwarz2013">F. Schwarz, Loewy Decomposition of Linear Differential Equations, Springer, 2013.</ref> Furthermore, the Janet basis of a module allows to read off a Janet basis for the syzygy module.<ref name="PleskenRobertz" />

Janet's algorithm has been implemented in Maple.<ref name="ZhangLi">S. Zhang, Z. Li, An Implementation for the Algorithm of Janet bases of Linear Differential Ideals in the Maple System, Acta Mathematicae Applicatae Sinica, English Series, '''20''', pages 605–616 (2004)</ref>
